idea.body: Some counting questions do not have one clean rule for the whole thing, but they split neatly into a few cases that do not overlap. Count each case on its own, then add the cases together for the total. A game lets you pick one accessory for a robot: one of 4 hat styles, or one of 6 badge styles, never both at once. A hat pick and a badge pick can never be the same choice, so the two cases do not overlap. The total is 4 plus 6, which is 10 accessories in all. The two traps are forgetting a case, and adding two cases that actually share some outcomes.

figure.alt: A root labelled all outcomes branching into case 1 and case 2, with a note to add the cases.

items.s: Add the cases for the total

workedExample.prompt: A game lets player one pick one of 3 avatar shapes: circle, square, or triangle. Player two then picks a different shape from the remaining two. How many pairs of shapes are possible?
steps: Split the count into 3 cases, one for each shape player one could pick.
In every case, player two then has exactly 2 remaining shapes to choose from.
Each of the 3 cases contributes 2 pairs, so the cases add to 3 times 2.
3 times 2 is 6 possible pairs of shapes.

figure.alt: A root labelled player one branching into circle, square and triangle, each leading to 2 choices, totalling 6 pairs.

ways.name: Split and add the cases
ways.when: Use this when a choice comes from one non-overlapping group or another, never both.
steps: A rover's tool bay offers one attachment: 5 scoop types or 3 drill types.
No attachment belongs to both groups, so the two cases never overlap.
Count each case on its own: 5 scoops, 3 drills.
Add the cases together: 5 plus 3 is 8 choices in all.
ways.example: A rover picks one attachment: 5 scoop types or 3 drill types. How many choices in all?
ways.trap: Multiplying the two case counts together instead of adding them.

figure.alt: A root labelled all attachments branching into scoops worth 5 and drills worth 3, adding to 8.

ways.name: The case-by-case table
ways.when: Use this when each case has its own separate rule, not one multiplication for everything.
steps: Split two-digit numbers with digits adding to 16 by the tens digit.
Tens digit 7 needs ones digit 9, giving 79.
Tens digit 8 needs ones digit 8, giving 88.
Tens digit 9 needs ones digit 7, giving 97.
That is 3 cases, one number each, so 3 in all.
ways.example: How many two-digit numbers have digits that add up to 16?
ways.trap: Trying tens digits below 7, which would need a ones digit bigger than 9.

figure.alt: Three stacked lines showing tens digit, ones digit and the resulting number for each case, then the total.

ways.name: The case tree
ways.when: Use this when you want to see every case branch out before counting the leaves.
steps: Split by what the first die shows, 1 to 4, since higher values leave no valid second die.
First die 1 needs second die 4; first die 2 needs 3; first die 3 needs 2; first die 4 needs 1.
Each of the 4 branches contributes exactly 1 way.
ways.example: Two dice are rolled. In how many ways can the two numbers add up to 5?
ways.trap: Counting first die 5 or 6 as a branch, even though no valid second die exists for them.

figure.alt: A tree with root first die branching into 1, 2, 3, 4, each leading to 1 way, totalling 4 ways.

frames.caption: Roll two dice for a sum of 5.
Split by what the first die shows.
Each first die pairs with one second.
Each of the 4 branches gives 1 way.

bank.prompt: How many two-digit numbers have digits that add up to 8?
explanation: Split by the tens digit, from 1 to 9. Each tens digit leaves exactly one ones digit to make the sum, if that digit is 0 to 9.
Tens digit 1 needs 7, and so on up to tens digit 8, which needs 0.
The working numbers are 17, 26, 35, 44, 53, 62, 71, 80.
That is 8 cases with one number each, so 8.
bank.useAgain: when a digit-sum condition splits naturally into one case per digit choice.
hints: Split the count into cases by the tens digit.
For each tens digit, check whether a matching ones digit from 0 to 9 exists.
bank.socraticHint: For a two-digit number with digit sum 8, does every choice of tens digit give a valid ones digit?

bank.prompt: Two dice are rolled. In how many ways can the two numbers add up to 5?
explanation: Split by what the first die shows, 1 to 6. Each case leaves exactly one value for the second die, if that value is 1 to 6.
The pairs that work are 1 and 4, 2 and 3, 3 and 2, 4 and 1.
That is 4 cases with one pair each, so 4.
The trap is counting 2 and 3 as the same as 3 and 2; they are different rolls.
bank.useAgain: when a two-part total splits naturally into one case per value of the first part.
hints: Try every value from 1 to 6 for the first die.
For each one, check if 5 minus that value is also a value from 1 to 6.
bank.socraticHint: Do all six cases for the first die give a valid second-die value, or only some?
